summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers can be used on 3G CDMA cellular networks. Mobile IPv6 is used there to keep connectivity as the device moves between access routers, but the usual handover steps cause delay. This informational document explains how to shorten that delay so connections are interrupted less.

eli5.summary: Moving between phone towers can make a call stutter. This explains how to prepare the next tower in advance on a particular type of mobile network, so the hand-off is smoother.

how to reduce handover latency in 3g cdma
subtitle: Speeding up handovers in cellular networks.

tldr.problem: In 3G CDMA networks, Mobile IPv6 handover requires the mobile node to acquire a new address and re-register with the home agent, causing noticeable delay and packet loss during voice or video calls.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adapts Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover to 3G CDMA by using air-interface pilot signals as handover triggers, providing handover assist information (network IDs) to identify the next access router, and adding buffer management flags.
tldr.outcome: Handover latency is reduced, enabling seamless VoIP and video calls over mobile IPv6 in 3G CDMA networks.

facts.value: B flag in FBU, R flag in PrRtAdv

today: RFC 5271 is informational, providing guidance for implementing Mobile IPv6 fast handover in 3G CDMA networks. It was published in June 2008. Today, 3G CDMA deployment remains active in some regions, and the extension mechanisms defined in the RFC (options for network identifiers and mobile node identifiers) are reused in newer mobility standards and provide a foundation for other handover optimizations.

sections.title: The Challenge of Mobile IPv6 in 3G
sections.content:
3G CDMA networks use Mobile IPv6 to maintain connectivity when a mobile node moves between access routers (called PDSNs in CDMA terminology). However, the standard MIPv6 handover sequence is slow: the MN must detect movement, acquire a new care-of address, perform address autoconfiguration, and send a binding update to the home agent. During this time, data packets destined for the MN are lost.

The RFC notes that 3G CDMA is substantially different from WiFi: the radio access network uses pilots (broadcast signals) to help the MN measure signal strength and identify nearby sectors. The network can use these pilot measurements to predict handover and prepare the next access router in advance. This prediction opportunity is the key to reducing handover delay.
sections.eli5: Your phone hears pilot signals from neighboring towers. The network knows from these signals which tower you will reach next. So it can prepare that tower before you arrive, like a relay team passing the baton before the runner fully reaches the handoff zone.

sections.title: 3G CDMA Handover Signals
sections.content:
In 3G CDMA, a mobile node maintains a set of pilot channels from nearby base stations and measures the signal strength (C/I, carrier-to-interference ratio) of each. When a neighbor pilot's strength exceeds the serving pilot, the MN sends a measurement report to the network. The network then decides whether to initiate handover.

Handover Assist Information includes the ANID (Access Network Identifier, composed of System ID, Network ID, and Packet Zone ID) and Sector ID. This information helps the serving access router identify which access network (and thus which PDSN) will serve the MN next.

The network can also provide this information to the MN via MN-ID option (carrying IMSI or NAI) and Handover Assist Information option (carrying ANID or Sector ID) in FMIPv6 messages. These options allow the MN to identify the next network without relying on link-layer addresses, which may not be unique in 3G CDMA.
sections.eli5: The phone measures pilot strength from towers. When a new tower looks stronger, the phone reports it. The network sends codes identifying that tower's network. The phone uses these codes to find the new router and prepare its new address.

sections.title: Predictive and Reactive Fast Handover
sections.content:
Predictive mode is the preferred approach in 3G CDMA because the network controls handover timing via pilot measurements. The MN sends RtSolPr with handover assist information to the PAR. The PAR identifies the NAR and sends back a PrRtAdv. The MN then formulates a temporary new care-of address (NCoA) and sends FBU. The PAR sets a tunnel to the NAR, which starts buffering packets. Critically, the PAR MUST send HI with the 'S' flag set, indicating that the NAR should assign the correct NCoA because the MN's temporary address may use the wrong prefix.

Reactive mode is used if the network does not support predictive mode (indicated by the 'R' flag in PrRtAdv). The PAR buffers packets when it receives FBU or when the lower layer signals link closure. The MN performs 802.1x attachment to the new network, then sends UNA and FBU to complete the handover. A new flag 'B' in the FBU tells the PAR to buffer packets.
sections.eli5: Predictive: the network warns the old router to prepare a tunnel before the phone switches. Reactive: if preparation is not ready, the old router buffers data and hands it over when the phone arrives at the new router.

sections.title: Attachment and Bootstrapping
sections.content:
When the MN attaches to a new access network in 3G CDMA, it establishes a link-layer connection (PPP) and exchanges several messages: LCP (Link Control Protocol), authentication (CHAP/PAP), IPv6CP (to negotiate interface ID), RA (router advertisement with prefix), and DHCPv6 (to learn the home agent address). This sequence takes considerable time.

The RFC notes that if the MN already has a temporary NCoA from the FBU/HAck exchange, several steps can be skipped: the router advertisement is not needed because the prefix is already known. This reduces attachment time, allowing predictive mode to deliver packets with lower latency.
sections.eli5: Setting up a connection on the new network normally takes many steps. But if the old router already sent the new address during preparation, those steps can be skipped.

sections.title: Message Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC defines three new message extensions:

Handover Assist Information Option (Type 29): Carries ANID or Sector ID to help the old router identify the new access network without relying on link-layer addresses. Option-Code 1 is ANID (5 octets), and Option-Code 2 is Sector ID (128 bits).

Mobile Node Identifier Option (Type 30): Carries a mobile node identifier such as IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity) or NAI (Network Access Identifier) instead of a link-layer address. Option-Code 1 is NAI, and Option-Code 2 is IMSI.

New Flags: The FBU message gains a 'B' flag to request buffering at the PAR in reactive mode. The PrRtAdv message gains an 'R' flag to indicate whether the network supports only reactive mode (R flag set) or both predictive and reactive mode.
sections.eli5: 3G networks need to pass special information in handover messages: network IDs, phone IDs, and flags asking the old router to buffer data.
